newsitem.title: UK: Broad EMU does not imply soft euro -BoE official.
newsitem.headline: Broad EMU does not imply soft euro -BoE official.

text.p: A large starting line-up for EMU in Janaury 1999 does not necessarily imply a 'soft' euro, Bank of England executive director Ian Plenderleith told bankers at a conference here on Tuesday.
"Most (commentators) are taking the view that a wider starting group implies a softer euro. That sounds too simplistic," Plenderleith said.
Such an argument implied inflationary pressures would be allowed to build up. "But the ECB (European Central Bank) would act on that with higher rates," he said.
Plenderleith is a member of the BoE's monetary policy committee which sets British interest rates.
Instead, much would depend on "policies adopted on fiscal and monetary matters," Plenderleith said.
He continued: "It is sensible to expect EMU to go ahead on time whatever its construction...Monetary union in Europe would be a tremendous step forward".

The third stage of European economic and monetary union, including the introduction of the European Union's planned single currency, the euro, is prescribed by EU law to take place no later than January 1, 1999.
Britain's finance minister Gordon Brown has said it was unlikely to join at the first time of asking whether or not it meets the qualifying criteria.
